# Comparisons

Side-by-side analyses placing VeVe against the platforms it is most often measured against. Each page
is web-researched with cited sources; anything the sources disagree on is flagged in an
`Unverified` callout rather than smoothed over.

## Licensed-collectibles platforms

- [[veve-vs-candy-digital|VeVe vs Candy Digital]] — the MLB/Netflix licensed platform on Palm. Closest
  competitor by model; notably has **no public market API**, which is why the app's Candy tab is dark.
- [[veve-vs-droppp|VeVe vs Droppp]] — Funko's digital-pop platform on WAX, with redeemable physical items.

## Different model entirely

- [[veve-vs-open-nft-marketplaces|VeVe vs open NFT marketplaces]] — walled-garden licensed collectibles
  versus OpenSea / Magic Eden / Blur and open PFP collections: custody, IP rights, who sets scarcity,
  royalties, and why floor-based marketcaps are not comparable to trade-based ones.

## Related

- [[nft/_index|NFT Collections]] — 20 researched non-VeVe collections
- [[platform/market-structure|Market Structure]] — how VeVe's own two venues differ
- [[platform/_index|Platform Reference]]

comparisons/veve-vs-candy-digital.md:
# VeVe vs Candy Digital

**Candy Digital** is the closest structural analogue to [[platform/veve|VeVe]]: a licensed digital-collectibles storefront built on blue-chip IP (MLB, DC, WWE, Netflix, Getty Images) rather than on generative PFP art. The two platforms answered the same question — *how do you sell an officially licensed collectible to a non-crypto fan?* — and arrived at almost opposite answers on chain, custody, marketplace and, critically for this project, **data**.

The comparison also has a moving part: Candy is **no longer on Palm**. Palm (an Ethereum-compatible sidechain) was Candy's mint chain from 2021 — the 2026 end date is inference, see the flag below; in April 2026 Candy announced a migration to **Solana** on Metaplex Core, which ran May–June 2026. Everything below is dated accordingly.

## At a glance

| | VeVe / Collect | Candy Digital |
|---|---|---|
| **Operator** | [[platform/ecomi|ECOMI, rebranding to Collect]] (Auckland, NZ) | Candy Digital — acquired by **Futureverse**, announced 2025-04-16 |
| **Launched** | 2018 (ECOMI app); first Marvel NFT Aug 2021 | June 2021 (launched by Fanatics with Mike Novogratz / Galaxy and Gary Vaynerchuk) |
| **Chain (now)** | **Collect Chain** (EVM); OMI settlement on **Base** | **Solana**, Metaplex Core (migrated May–Jun 2026) |
| **Chain (before)** | GoChain → Immutable X (2021) → Collect Chain (~early 2026) | **Palm** — Ethereum-compatible sidechain, 2021 → 2026 |
| **Primary sales** | Timed [[platform/drops|drops]] in the app, priced in [[Gems]] (1 Gem = US$1) | Pack drops on candy.io, credit/debit card + Candy platform credits |
| **Secondary market** | **In-house**: VeVe in-app market (Gems) **+ StackR** on Base (OMI) | Opened **2026-07-24** — sellers list from candy.io, but trades settle on **Magic Eden** in SOL (Tensor also linked per collection) |
| **Client** | Mobile-first app (iOS/Android) + web app | Web only (candy.io); no mobile app documented |
| **Custody** | Platform-held collectibles; self-custody **StackR Wallet** for OMI | Candy-generated **self-custody Solana wallet**; private key exportable to Phantom |
| **Loyalty / score layer** | [[Master Collector Points|Master Collector Points]] (daily, holding-based) | **Diamond Economy** (2026-06) — platform credits earned by *burning* collectibles, unlocking tiered Gold/Diamond auctions and quests |
| **Public market API** | No official public API, but a public on-chain explorer (collectscan.com) + public per-collectible blog pages | **No documented public market API** |
| **Sport licences** | None | MLB, NASCAR (as "Racing"), WWE |

## Licensors

Candy's catalogue is **sports-first with a comics anchor**; VeVe's is **entertainment/comics/pop-culture with no sports at all**. That is the single biggest content difference between them, and it means the two are barely competitors on shelf space.

Candy's own collections index (retrieved 2026-07-30) exposes brand facets with counts:

| Candy brand facet | Collections |
|---|--:|
| DC | 281 |
| MLB | 84 |
| Getty Images | 7 |
| Racing (NASCAR) | 7 |
| WWE | 4 |
| Netflix (Stranger Things) | 3 |
| Sweet Futures | 3 |
| Other (Palm Garden, Sex Pistols, CandyCorp, MCNY) | 5 |
| **Total** | **394** |

The DC weighting is a legacy of the **Palm NFT Studio merger (2023-06-29)** — Palm brought Warner Bros. Discovery / DC Comics and Universal Music Group client work, Candy brought MLB, NASCAR, WWE, Netflix and Getty Images. The combined company kept the Candy name under CEO Scott Lawin.

**DC is the only licensor the two platforms share.** VeVe's DC line runs to 82 catalogued collectibles plus a large comics catalogue; see [[domains/dc|DC]]. VeVe's other anchors (Marvel, Star Wars, Disney, Pixar, TMNT, Star Trek, Street Fighter, Ultraman, plus a large real-world-brand and artist-collab tier) have no Candy counterpart.

> [!note] Not a like-for-like count
> Candy's 394 "collections" and this wiki's 1,865 taxonomy collections are different units. Candy counts a drop/series; this wiki's `collections` layer is a 15-axis taxonomy over ~2,850 collectibles and ~3,856 comic issues. Do not read 394 vs 1,865 as a size ratio.

## Chain and custody

VeVe moved GoChain → Immutable X → **Collect Chain**, its own EVM chain, with `collectscan.com` as the public explorer. OMI, the ecosystem token, lives on **Base**, where **StackR** runs the OMI-denominated secondary market and the self-custody StackR Wallet (StackR sponsors gas, so a collector never needs ETH). Collectibles themselves are held in the platform account; [[Gems]] are closed-loop and non-withdrawable since 2025-11-19.

Candy went the other way in 2026. Its migration explicitly optimises for **self-custody and third-party liquidity**: assets land in a Candy-generated Solana wallet, media is pinned to **Arweave**, royalties are enforced via **Metaplex Core**, and Candy's stated path is for fans to reveal the private key and import the wallet into **Phantom**. Candy pays the technical-services fee for qualifying "Active Fans."

The migration mechanics, from Candy's own posts:

| Date (2026) | Event |
|---|---|
| Apr 22 | Move to Solana announced |
| May 12–20 | **Pre-migration burn window** — $0.50 in Candy platform credit per burned asset; credits non-transferable, expire 2027-05-31 |
| May 20 | "Active Fan" cutoff (log in + review collection) |
| May 21 | Migration begins, in batches over multiple days |
| Jun 1 | Refreshed candy.io live — wallet visibility, migration status, mandatory 2FA, updated Terms |
| ~Jun 8 | Secondary trading *targeted* to open for migrated legacy assets — slipped |
| Jul 24 | Secondary market actually opens — list from candy.io, trade on Magic Eden in SOL |
| Dec 31 | Legacy-system assets accessible on-platform "until at least" this date |

Burn-for-credit was not a one-off migration window. It carried on after the migration as the **Diamond Economy** (2026-06-17: 2026 collectibles earn $0.50 in platform credit, legacy ones $0.25, feeding tiered Gold/Diamond auctions). It has **no VeVe equivalent** — VeVe has never offered to retire editions in exchange for store credit, and doing so would collide with the fixed `edition_size` that underpins [[Rarity and Editions|rarity]] and [[platform/floor-prices|floor pricing]].

> [!warning] Unverified — Solana vs The Root Network
> Futureverse's acquisition announcement (2025-04-16) said Candy's assets would be integrated into **The Root Network**, Futureverse's own layer-1. Candy's own 2026 posts describe the collectibles moving to **Solana** with Metaplex Core, and candy.io now carries a "Solana powered" badge. No source found reconciles the two statements — whether The Root Network plan was dropped, deferred, or is meant to sit alongside Solana is unclear.

> [!warning] Partly unverified — "Palm" as Candy's old chain
> The chain name is well sourced for the Palm era: Decrypt (2021-10-21) states Candy "mints its NFTs on Palm, an Ethereum sidechain," and Ledger Insights repeats "an Ethereum compatible sidechain" at the 2023 merger. What is **not** confirmed is the end date — Candy's 2026 migration posts never name the chain they migrated *from*, only that collectibles are moving to Solana. Treat "Palm through 2026" as inference, not a sourced fact.

## Marketplace model

This is the sharpest divide.

- **VeVe runs its own secondary market.** Listing, buying and the floor all live inside the app, denominated in Gems, with StackR as a parallel OMI-denominated venue on Base. Two markets, both attributable to specific collectibles, both feeding [[platform/record-sales|record sales]] and [[platform/floor-prices|floor prices]].
- **Candy mostly does not.** Its secondary market opened **2026-07-24**: a seller can list straight from their candy.io collection, but the order book, the buyer flow and settlement all happen on **Magic Eden**, denominated in SOL (Tensor is also linked per collection). Candy keeps royalty enforcement (via Metaplex Core) and now owns the listing UX, but price discovery still sits on a third-party venue.

The consequence: Candy's price history is scattered across third-party venues under Solana collection mint addresses, while VeVe's is concentrated in two venues it controls.

## App vs web

VeVe is **app-first** — a 3D/AR viewer, Showrooms, an in-app comic reader, [[Blind Box|blind boxes]] with queue mechanics, and a web app mainly used to buy Gems without app-store fees. The collectible is something you *open and display*.

Candy is **web-first** and has no documented mobile app. The 2026 site is deliberately thin: account access, collection visibility, migration status, wallet info, asset detail pages. The collectible is something you *hold in a wallet* and trade elsewhere. Candy's own framing on the 2026 site is "Pull. Chase. Own." and "Wallet-native" — pack-ripping plus custody, not a showroom.

## Data availability

For this project's purposes, the two platforms are not comparable at all.

| | VeVe / Collect | Candy Digital |
|---|---|---|
| Per-item public metadata | Yes — `veve.me/blog/collectibles/<slug>` gives drop date, edition size, rarity, list price in Gems, reserved count, first public mint | Collection-level only (name, brand, item count, mint address) |
| Public on-chain explorer | Yes — collectscan.com (Collect Chain) | Solana public RPC / explorers, but no Candy-branded explorer |
| Public sale/price feed | Effectively yes — this wiki mirrors **302,286 real completed sales since 2025-07-12** across VeVe (Gems) and StackR (OMI) | **Not from Candy** — since 2026-07-24 trades settle on Magic Eden, so prices are readable only via third-party Solana APIs, per collection mint |
| Documented public API | No official API, but a stable public surface | **No** — Candy's FAQ documents no API, developer tools or program docs |

> [!note] Why the app's Candy tab is disabled
> The community app carries a Candy tab that is rendered **disabled on purpose** (`app/nft.html`, the tab is emitted with `disabled title="Candy Digital — research in progress (no public market API yet)"`). There is no Candy-published market or price API to read, and Candy's secondary market (open since 2026-07-24) settles on Magic Eden rather than on a Candy-run venue, so any Candy floor/sales panel would have to be reconstructed from third-party Solana marketplace APIs per collection mint. Until that is built and verified, the tab stays dark rather than showing a guess. This matches the wiki's `# TODO`-over-a-guess rule.

## Corporate churn — the other asymmetry

Candy has changed owner three times in five years; VeVe has had one operator throughout.

| Date | Candy Digital |
|---|---|
| 2021-06 | Launched by Fanatics with Mike Novogratz (Galaxy) and Gary Vaynerchuk |
| 2021-10 | ~$100M raise at a reported $1.5B valuation |
| 2023-01 | Fanatics divests its 60% stake to a group led by Galaxy Digital (with ConsenSys Mesh and 10T Holdings); Michael Rubin's internal email says NFTs are "unlikely to be sustainable or profitable as a standalone business" — *"imploding NFT market" is CNBC/trade-press phrasing, not a Rubin quote* |
| 2023-06-29 | Merger with Palm NFT Studio; ~30 layoffs; Candy brand retained |
| 2025-04-16 | **Futureverse acquires Candy Digital** — 4M+ collectibles, 1.5M accounts cited; terms undisclosed |
| 2026 | Migration off the legacy chain to Solana |

VeVe's equivalent instability is technical rather than corporate — three chains in five years — but the operator, the app, the currency ([[Gems]]) and the catalogue have been continuous. That continuity is exactly what makes a 300k-sale price history possible.

## What VeVe does differently

1. **It owns its secondary market.** Price discovery happens inside VeVe (Gems) and on StackR (OMI), not on a generic marketplace. Candy outsources price discovery to Magic Eden / Tensor — since 2026-07-24 fronted by a listing tool on candy.io — and keeps royalties.
2. **It ships a product, not a wallet.** 3D/AR viewing, Showrooms, an in-app comic reader and blind-box drop theatre. Candy's 2026 site is a storefront plus a custody view.
3. **It publishes per-item primary-sale facts.** Edition size, rarity, Gem list price, reserved count and first public mint are public per collectible — the substrate this entire wiki is built on. Candy publishes collection-level metadata only.
4. **It has a holding-based score economy.** [[Master Collector Points|MCP]] rewards *holding* rather than spending, with published diminishing returns on comic duplicates for Rare / Ultra Rare / Secret Rare. Candy's published equivalent, the **Diamond Economy**, rewards *burning* rather than holding.
5. **Fixed supply, never retired.** VeVe's `edition_size` is fixed and editions below the lowest public mint are reserved by VeVe, not destroyed. Candy actively **burns** collectibles for platform credit — during the 2026 pre-migration window, and on an ongoing basis under the Diamond Economy.
6. **Entertainment IP, not sports rights.** ~50+ licensors across Marvel, Star Wars, Disney, DC, TMNT and a deep artist-collab tier; zero sports leagues. Candy's centre of gravity is MLB, NASCAR and WWE.

Where Candy is genuinely ahead: **self-custody**. A migrated Candy asset can leave the platform into Phantom and trade on open Solana venues. A VeVe collectible cannot leave the ecosystem the same way, and Gems have been non-withdrawable since 2025-11-19.

comparisons/veve-vs-droppp.md:
# VeVe vs. Droppp

**Droppp** was the licensed digital-collectibles platform behind **Funko Digital Pop!** — animated collectible cards on the **WAX** blockchain, many of which could be redeemed for a physical Funko Pop! vinyl figure. It is the closest structural competitor VeVe ever had, and the most useful one to study, because **Funko sunset Droppp on 31 May 2026** while [[platform/veve|VeVe]] kept operating. This page compares the two models — licensors, physical redemption, chain, secondary market, rarity — and then asks what the two designs actually optimised for.

> [!note] Droppp is closed
> As of this writing (2026-07-30) `droppp.io` 301-redirects to Funko's sunset announcement. Droppp accounts and wallets were disabled **31 May 2026, 11:59:59 PM PST**. Digital Pop! tokens themselves survive on WAX for collectors who transferred them out to an external WAX wallet (Funko named AtomicHub) before the deadline; USDC left in a Droppp wallet had to be withdrawn by the same deadline. Everything below describing Droppp is therefore written in the past tense.

## At a glance

| | **VeVe / Collect** | **Droppp (Funko Digital Pop!)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Operator** | **ECOMI** — see [[platform/ecomi\|ECOMI]]. ("Collect" is the new *blockchain*, not a corporate rebrand: VeVe's own announcement says "VeVe isn't going anywhere.") | Droppp, built and run with **TokenWave** for Funko (Funko took a majority stake in TokenWave in Apr 2021) |
| **Status (2026-07)** | Active | **Sunset 31 May 2026** |
| **Launched** | Development began 2018 as "ECOMI Collect"; renamed VeVe and released to app stores **end of 2020**, Market opened early 2021; first Marvel NFT **7 Aug 2021** | Digital Pop! launched **2021**; droppp.io opened 2021 |
| **Product form** | 3D "Premium Collectibles," digital comics, digital art — AR + showroom viewing | 2D animated collectible **cards** ("Digital Pop!"), rarer tiers with more elaborate animation |
| **Licensing posture** | Licenses **direct from ~50+ rights-holders** (Marvel, DC, Star Wars, Disney, Stanley Gibbons…) | Built on **Funko's own** license portfolio — Disney, DC, Marvel, Star Wars, Harry Potter, TMNT, Transformers, Star Trek, My Little Pony |
| **Primary sale** | Timed [[platform/drops\|drops]], incl. [[Blind Box\|blind boxes]]; waitlist/queue; priced in [[Gems]] (1 Gem = US$1) | **Packs**: standard 5 items US$9.99, premium 15 items US$29.99 (premium raised to **17 items at the same price** in 2024) — bought with card / Apple Pay / Google Pay |
| **Chain** | GoChain → Immutable X (migration completed Dec 2021) → **Collect Chain** (Phase 1 announced for Jan 2026; **full migration completed 1 Apr 2026**) | **WAX** (Worldwide Asset eXchange), an NFT-focused public chain |
| **Secondary market** | In-app [[platform/marketplace\|Market]] in Gems, **plus StackR** (Base) settling in [[OMI Token\|OMI]] | Droppp Marketplace (from Oct 2023), settling in **USDC**; also tradeable on WAX venues such as AtomicHub |
| **Rarity ladder** | 5 tiers: Common · Uncommon · Rare · Ultra Rare · **Secret Rare** | 6 core tiers: Common · Uncommon · Rare · Epic · **Legendary** · **Grail** — some collections also carried *1 of 1* and *Series* tiers |
| **Physical redemption** | **Occasional, licensor-specific "phygital"** drops (e.g. Stanley Gibbons stamps) | **Core to the model** — Grail/Legendary or a completed Royalty Set earned a Redemption Token for a physical Pop! |
| **Loyalty layer** | [[Master Collector Points\|MCP]] — daily points for *holding* | Gamified "Arcade" seasons *(see flag below)* |
| **KYC** | Not required to join a waitlist or buy; **required to sell in the Market and to use Payout**; verified users get priority in waitlist reservations | Required to use the secondary marketplace |

## The two models

The headline difference is **what the digital object is for**.

On Droppp the digital card was substantially a **claim ticket**. You bought a pack, you hoped for a Grail or a Legendary — or you ground out one card of each of Common/Uncommon/Rare/Epic to complete a "Royalty Set" — and the reward was a **physical, limited Funko Pop! shipped to your door**. The digital art was real and collectors genuinely liked it, but the economics were anchored to a physical object with an established resale market. That anchoring is why secondary prices for ordinary cards could sit under a dollar while the set-completion route still made sense: an outside observer reported finishing a set and earning the Royalty Pop for under $50.

On VeVe the digital object is **the** collectible. There is no physical counterpart for the overwhelming majority of the catalogue (~2,850 collectibles and ~3,856 comic issues in this wiki's index), and value is generated endogenously — by [[Rarity and Editions|edition size and mint number]], by [[Secret Rare]] scarcity, by brand demand, and by the [[Master Collector Points|MCP]] program that pays you for *holding* rather than flipping. VeVe's [[platform/record-sales|record sales]] show what that produces at the top end: five-figure completed sales for single digital editions, an order of magnitude beyond anything a redeemable vinyl figure supports.

Those are different bets. Droppp's bet was that **a physical redemption makes a digital collectible legible** to a mainstream Funko collector — low friction, low price, obvious value floor. VeVe's bet is that a deep licensed catalogue plus real scarcity mechanics plus a display experience (AR, showroom) is enough on its own. The Droppp bet was the safer one on paper and it is the one that got switched off. **Funko published no reason**: its sunset notice calls the decision "difficult" and offers no business rationale, and coverage at the time noted Funko had not explained itself. The CEO explanation is *reporting, not a Funko statement* — Nerdbeak attributes the closure to new CEO Josh Simon (appointed 12 Aug 2025, effective 1 Sep 2025) steering back toward core physical product. Taken at that discount, it still reads as a *strategic* failure mode rather than an economic one, and it is the single most transferable lesson here: on Droppp the platform's survival depended on one licensor's corporate priorities, because the licensor *was* the platform's reason to exist. VeVe's ~50+ independent licensor relationships are structurally less fragile in exactly that way — and correspondingly more expensive and more exposed to per-licensor rights churn (see the licensor flags throughout this wiki).

## Redeemable physicals, compared

Droppp's redemption flow was systematic and repeatable:

- Pull a **Grail** or **Legendary**, or assemble a **Royalty Set** (one each of Common, Uncommon, Rare, Epic) → you qualify for a **Redemption Token**.
- Qualification was determined by a **snapshot ~120 days after each series dropped**, so cards were freely tradeable up to that point — the snapshot, not the purchase, decided who got the figure.
- Redemption Tokens were deposited into eligible WAX accounts, holders had **30 days** to redeem, and the physical Pop! shipped from there.

VeVe does the same *thing* only occasionally, and always as a licensor-driven special. The clearest worked example in this wiki is the **Stanley Gibbons** philatelic partnership, where the physical item is not a reproduction but a genuine 19th-century artifact:

| VeVe phygital drop | Qualifying tier | Physical reward |
|---|---|---|
| [[stanley-gibbons-penny-red-nk\|Stanley Gibbons 1841 Penny Red — NK]] (drop 2025-07-20, 110 editions, 10 Gems) | Secret Rare only | One of **100** original 1841 Penny Red NK physical stamps |
| [[stanley-gibbons-penny-black-be-cf-block\|Stanley Gibbons 1840 Penny Black — BE-CF block]] (drop 2024-10-06, 150 editions, 10 Gems) | Secret Rare only | One of **150** original 1840 Penny Black stamps in a VeVe-exclusive case |

Two things follow. First, **scope**: on Droppp redemption was the point of nearly every drop; on VeVe it is a garnish on a handful of drops from one or two licensors (see [[stanley-gibbons-stamps|Stanley Gibbons]]). Second, **odds**: Droppp gave you multiple routes to a physical (chase pull *or* patient set completion, the latter purchasable on the secondary market); VeVe's phygital route is chase-pull-only, gated behind a Secret Rare in a [[Blind Box|blind box]] — 110 editions out of an 8,633-edition Penny Red drop, and only 100 of those 110 carried a stamp (10 were withheld for licensor/promotional use).

## Rarity models

The ladders look parallel but are not equivalent, and it is a mistake to map them one-to-one:

| Position | VeVe | Droppp |
|---|---|---|
| Base | Common | Common |
| | Uncommon | Uncommon |
| | Rare | Rare |
| | — | Epic |
| Upper | Ultra Rare | Legendary |
| Chase | **Secret Rare** | **Grail** |

The real difference is what the tier *does*:

- **VeVe** — rarity is not a strict function of edition size, and every copy carries a **mint number** within a fixed, published edition size. Rarity plus low mint feed [[Master Collector Points|MCP]] accrual directly (Secret Rare pays the most per day) and drive secondary premiums. Editions below the lowest public mint are held back by VeVe (often #1–40, varies per item), which is why "lowest public mint" is a tracked field in this wiki, not a constant. See [[Significant Mints]].
- **Droppp** — rarity gated **redemption eligibility** and animation quality. Legendary and Grail were the tiers that entitled you to a physical figure; Epic existed largely as the fourth rung you needed for a Royalty Set. Cards carried WAX mint numbers and collectors did prize low ones, but the mint number was not wired into a points economy the way VeVe's is.

## Chain, custody and portability

This is where the comparison flatters Droppp and it is worth being honest about it.

Droppp was built on **WAX**, a public NFT chain, and the shutdown proved the point: the platform died and the assets did not. Collectors who moved their Digital Pop! to an external WAX wallet still own them today, tradeable on venues Funko does not control.

VeVe's position is more custodial. Collectibles migrated to **Collect Chain** (a public EVM ledger), and OMI moved to **Base**, where the **StackR** wallet is genuinely self-custody for the *token* — you hold OMI yourself, and StackR sponsors gas on its Base OMI transactions so you never need a second asset to trade (StackR's own FAQ notes network gas still applies on deposits/withdrawals). But holding the *collectible* in a wallet you control is a separate, later step.

> [!warning] Announced, not shipped — VeVe collectible self-custody
> This is now confirmed from VeVe's own posts, not just reporting. The Collect announcement puts self-custody in **Phase 2**: "Soon, you'll be able to self-custody your VeVe collectibles… outside of the VeVe app," rolling out after Phase 1. Phase 1 was announced for January 2026; the **full migration actually completed 1 April 2026**, and that post still says Collect only "*plans* to introduce optional self-custody" in phase two. **No Phase 2 date has been published**, and no live collectible-withdrawal path is documented. Treat "VeVe collectibles are self-custodial" as **false today**; ship date `# TODO`.

The practical asymmetry: a Droppp collector's downside in a shutdown was inconvenience. A VeVe collector's exposure, until collectible self-custody actually ships, is closer to platform risk.

## Secondary market

| | VeVe | Droppp |
|---|---|---|
| **Venues** | In-app Market (Gems) + StackR on Base (OMI) | Droppp Marketplace (USDC) + open WAX venues (e.g. AtomicHub) |
| **Settlement asset** | [[Gems]] in-app (closed-loop, 1 Gem = US$1, non-withdrawable since 19 Nov 2025); [[OMI Token\|OMI]] on StackR | **USDC** (1:1 USD stablecoin) |
| **Fees** | Licensor + marketplace fee paid by seller; buyer's fee in OMI is **burned** — see [[platform/omi-economics\|OMI economics]] | Not published in the sources reviewed — `# TODO` |
| **Cash out** | Sell for OMI on StackR → swap → off-ramp; KYC required | Withdraw USDC to an exchange |
| **Access limits** | Regional availability varies | Marketplace excluded AK, HI, MN, NY and 18 countries; ID verification required. Pack sales were **not** subject to those marketplace restrictions |
| **Depth (measured)** | 300k+ real completed sales recorded since 2025-07-12 across both markets | Not measured here — `# TODO` |

Droppp's USDC settlement is arguably the cleaner design for a collector who wants an unambiguous dollar exit: list, sell, withdraw a stablecoin. VeVe's split — a closed-loop Gems economy in-app and an OMI-denominated market outside it — means the in-app price you see and the realisable value outside the app are quoted in different units, with a burn and a fee between them. That gap is a recurring source of confusion and is the reason this wiki treats in-app floors carefully (see [[platform/floor-prices|floor prices]]).

> [!warning] Unverified — Droppp Arcade, 2024 drop count, Exclusive portability
> - Droppp ran a gamified **"Arcade"** seasonal layer. Reporting says it was to be discontinued after **Season 2**, sourced to a Discord moderator rather than an official announcement. Mechanics unverified.
> - Funko's own retrospective confirms **20 Digital Pop! drops in 2023**. A "27 drops in 2024" figure appeared in search snippets attributed to Funko's blog but could not be confirmed on fetch — omitted from the tables above.
> - Droppp *Exclusive* items were historically restricted to transfers between Droppp `.dp` addresses only; that restriction was relaxed for the sunset. The Funko Support article documenting this **no longer resolves** (302 to a generic help centre), so the exact history of which items were portable when is `# TODO`.
> - Funko's own Digital Pop! FAQ (`digital.funko.com/faq`) returned **503** on 2026-07-30, consistent with the sunset, so tier definitions and pack mechanics above rest on third-party sources (WAX's own Medium, Funko's 2023/2024 blog posts) rather than the primary FAQ.

## Takeaways

1. **Redeemable physicals lower the barrier but cap the ceiling.** Droppp's Pop!-backed model made digital collecting instantly legible to a mainstream audience and kept prices low and rational. VeVe's purely digital model produced five-figure sales that a $12 vinyl figure can never underwrite.
2. **Platform risk sits where the licensing sits.** Droppp existed to sell one company's IP and ended at that company's discretion — Funko gave no public reason, which is itself the point. VeVe's multi-licensor catalogue is the more durable structure and the more operationally demanding one.
3. **Public-chain custody is the real insurance policy.** WAX portability is why Digital Pop! survived Droppp. Until collectible self-custody ships on Collect Chain, VeVe collectors do not have the equivalent.
4. **Settlement clarity matters to collectors.** USDC at 1:1 is easier to reason about than Gems-in / OMI-out with a burn in between.

comparisons/veve-vs-open-nft-marketplace.md:
# VeVe vs Open NFT Marketplaces

[[platform/veve|VeVe]] and the open NFT market solved two different problems and ended up structurally inverted on almost every axis. VeVe sells **licensed IP under a weak holder licence inside a walled garden**; open PFP collections such as [[nft/cryptopunks|CryptoPunks]] and [[nft/bored-ape-yacht-club|Bored Ape Yacht Club]] sell **unlicensed original art under a strong holder licence on open rails**. That inversion propagates all the way down into custody, who controls supply, whether creators actually get paid on resale, how price discovery works, and — the part most often got wrong — **which valuation numbers can be compared to which**.

The short version of the last point: a floor-based "market cap" and a trade-based sales record are different units. This wiki keeps them apart deliberately, and this page explains why.

## At a glance

| | VeVe / Collect | Open marketplaces + open PFP collections |
|---|---|---|
| **What is traded** | ~2,850 collectibles and ~3,856 comic issues, each a limited edition with many numbered copies | Collections of unique 1/1 tokens (usually 10,000 per collection) |
| **Venues** | Two, both operator-run: VeVe in-app market ([[Gems]]) + **StackR** on Base ([[OMI Token|OMI]]) | Many interchangeable front-ends over shared order books — OpenSea, Blur, Magic Eden, aggregators |
| **Chain** | [[platform/collect-chain|Collect Chain]] — one ERC-721 contract, `0xbcFEbA7A9dA14f5C9453bDA72E2098537867B3c7` | Ethereum / Solana / Bitcoin Ordinals; one contract or inscription set per collection |
| **Custody** | **Custodial** — VeVe generates the wallet; a collectible cannot leave the ecosystem. Optional self-custody is announced Phase 2, **not live** as of 2026-07-30 | **Self-custody** — the token sits in your wallet; marketplaces trade via approvals, not escrow |
| **Holder IP rights** | "personal, non-commercial, non-exclusive, non-transferable, non-sublicensable, revocable, limited" licence; IP stays with VeVe or the licensor | Ranges from full commercial rights (BAYC, CryptoPunks) to CC0 public domain ([[nft/moonbirds\|Moonbirds]] since Aug 2022) |
| **Who sets supply** | VeVe, per drop — `edition_size`, five rarity tiers, plus a reserved block below the lowest public mint | The contract, at deploy — fixed, countable, unchangeable by the creator |
| **Creator/licensor cut on resale** | **Unavoidable** — a licensor fee is charged on both VeVe and StackR sales | **Optional since 2022–23** on the major venues; re-enforceable only via opt-in standards like ERC-721C |
| **Price discovery** | Per collectible, and per mint number within it; split across two currencies | Per collection, with the floor as a live quote and deep bid-side pools |
| **Public trade data** | No official public API; on-chain ownership is public via `collectscan.com`; this project mirrors 300k+ real sales since 2025-07-12 | Public on-chain trade prints, plus marketplace and aggregator APIs |
| **Headline valuation metric in the wild** | Drop price in Gems, plus floor (a lowest *ask*) | "Market cap" = floor × supply, plus lifetime volume |

## Custody

**VeVe is custodial and says so.** VeVe generates a wallet per account (email login, no seed phrase), and a collector can read their own Collect Chain address, but cannot move a collectible out of the ecosystem. Optional self-custody was announced as Phase 2 of the Collect Chain migration in Nov 2025 and had not shipped as of 2026-07-30. The exit path is a sale on VeVe or StackR, not a transfer to a personal wallet. Details and on-chain evidence in [[platform/collect-chain|Collect Chain]].

**Open marketplaces never take custody at all.** The token stays in the owner's wallet and the marketplace executes against a signed order and a token approval. That single design choice is what makes the rest of the open market work — and what made royalties collapse (below), because if the venue doesn't hold the asset, the venue can't be forced to honour anything.

There is one real self-custody surface in the VeVe world: **StackR**. Per VeVe's own StackR FAQ, deposits and withdrawals of OMI run through the user's own Web3 wallet. So the *currency* can be self-custodied on Base while the *collectible* cannot.

> [!warning] Unverified — what listing does to on-chain ownership
> Roughly 80% of all non-mint VeVe transfers on Collect Chain pass through a single high-throughput address that holds relatively few editions at rest — the shape of a custodial marketplace escrow, which would mean the on-chain owner of a *listed* item is the platform rather than the collector. This is an inference from transfer patterns recorded in [[platform/collect-chain|Collect Chain]], not something VeVe has confirmed.

## IP rights — the actual inversion

VeVe's Terms of Use are unusually explicit. A buyer receives:

> "a personal, non-commercial, non-exclusive, non-transferable, non-sublicensable, revocable, limited license"

to view and use the Digital Property within the App, and "the Intellectual Property Rights in all Digital Properties remain with Us or the relevant VeVe Licensor." Ownership of a Collectible is stated to mean ownership of a **Token** plus that limited licence — "and does not denote any ownership of the Digital Property or other rights." The licence transfers to the buyer on a Market sale and expires immediately for the seller.

The open collections went the other way, and did so as a selling point:

| Collection | Holder IP posture | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| [[nft/bored-ape-yacht-club\|BAYC]] | Commercial-use rights to the individual ape image | Granted by Yuga Labs; enabled holder-run brands and merch |
| [[nft/cryptopunks\|CryptoPunks]] | Commercial rights granted to individual holders (2022) | Yuga Labs on acquiring the IP; IP sold on to the Infinite Node Foundation, May 2025 |
| [[nft/meebits\|Meebits]] | Full commercial rights to holders (2022) | IP later sold to The Meebit Company, Feb 2025 |
| [[nft/moonbirds\|Moonbirds]] | **CC0 public domain** since Aug 2022 | Divided holders who felt exclusive image rights were removed unilaterally |
| [[nft/bitcoin-puppets\|Bitcoin Puppets]] | Viral Public License — CC0-like copyleft | Derivatives and merch permitted by design |
| **VeVe** | Personal, non-commercial, revocable | The licensor never signs commercial rights over to fans |

This is the trade every collector on either side is actually making. **VeVe offers strong IP with weak rights; PFP projects offer weak IP with strong rights.** A Marvel or Disney licensing deal cannot grant a fan commercial use of Spider-Man, and no amount of chain design changes that — so the "you own your NFT's IP" pitch is structurally unavailable to a licensed platform. Conversely, a 2021 PFP collection had no pre-existing fandom to trade on, so granting commercial rights cost the issuer nothing it already had and bought cultural distribution it did not.

Note also that the IP itself is tradeable in the open model and has changed hands repeatedly (Larva Labs → Yuga Labs → Infinite Node Foundation for CryptoPunks; Yuga → MeebCo for Meebits; PROOF → Yuga → Orange Cap Games for Moonbirds). VeVe's licensors do not sell their IP to NFT companies; they licence it and take a cut.

## Who sets scarcity

**VeVe: scarcity is a business decision, published as a fact.**

- `edition_size` is set per drop by VeVe. Rarity runs Common · Uncommon · Rare · Ultra Rare · Secret Rare, and rarity is **not** a strict function of edition size — see [[Rarity and Editions]].
- A block of editions below the lowest public mint is **reserved by VeVe** (often #1–40, but it varies per item; the exact reserve count is off-chain).
- [[Blind Box]] contents are assigned server-side at reveal, so distribution within a drop is not observable in advance.
- VeVe can ship a further variant of the same subject as a *new* collectible with its own edition size. In [[platform/record-sales|record sales]], "Leonardo - Classic" and "Leonardo - Classic (Special Edition)" appear as separate items with separate prices.
- Supply is auditable **after** the fact: each token instance on Collect Chain carries `edition` and `totalEditions`. But the contract's `total_supply` reads `null`, so chain-side supply has to be reconstructed by paginating `/instances`.

**Open collections: scarcity is a contract constant.** Supply is fixed at deploy — 10,000 for CryptoPunks, 10,000 for BAYC — and anyone can count it at any time. Trait distributions are derivable from public metadata, which is why per-trait counts (9 Alien punks, 24 Ape, 88 Zombie; 46 Solid Gold fur apes) circulate as settled numbers rather than claims. What the creator *can* still change is the licence and the surrounding ecosystem: companion collections (MAYC, Oddities), staking mechanics, tokens.

The practical consequence for a collector: in an open collection you can verify scarcity yourself before buying. In VeVe you are trusting the operator's published edition size and reserve policy — verifiable on-chain today, but as an audit of what VeVe already did, not as a constraint on what VeVe can do next.

## Royalties — enforced by architecture vs. optional by competition

Open-market royalties were never enforced by the ERC-721 standard; they were enforced by marketplace convention, and the convention broke under competition.

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| 2022-10-15 | **Magic Eden** moves to optional creator royalties (full / half / none, default full) and waives its 2% platform fee, alongside a $1M Creator Monetization Hackathon |
| 2022-11 | **OpenSea** launches the **Operator Filter**, restricting sales to venues that enforce creator fees |
| 2023-02-17 | OpenSea goes to **0% marketplace fee** — "for a limited time" — and defaults collections without on-chain enforcement to optional royalties with a 0.5% floor — matching **Blur**, which charges 0% marketplace fee and enforces a 0.5% minimum royalty (full royalties for collections that blocklist OpenSea) |
| 2023-08-31 | OpenSea makes creator fees **optional for new collections** and **disables the Operator Filter** (both announced 2023-08-17, effective 2023-08-31); existing Operator-Filter collections stay enforced through 2024-02-29 |
| 2024-04 | OpenSea adds support for **ERC-721C** (Limit Break) — contract-level, enforceable creator earnings; Limit Break's Payment Processor + ERC-721C also underpin the Magic Eden × Yuga Labs Ethereum marketplace announced 2024-02-27 as royalty-enforcing |
| 2025-02-13 | **OS2** launches in open beta (out of beta 2025-05-29); OpenSea marketplace fee 0.5% |
| 2025-09-15 | OpenSea marketplace fee rises **0.5% → 1.0%**, half of it funding a pre-launch reward pool ahead of the SEA token |

**VeVe's licensor cut is not optional, and the reason is architectural, not moral.** There is no third venue. A VeVe collectible can be sold in the VeVe app or on StackR, and both apply a licensor fee. VeVe's StackR FAQ is explicit that a portion of the transaction fee goes to licensors, that **StackR itself takes no platform fee**, and that a percentage of every transaction fee is **burned** — and that the fee varies by licensor (Marvel, Disney named). VeVe's own current fee schedule (last updated 2025-08-13) says secondary-market fees "vary between Collectibles" and are shown to the seller at listing time; it publishes a **10% payout fee** on Gem withdrawals plus $1 (US) / $20 (international) bank transfer fees, but no secondary-market percentages.

> [!warning] Unverified — the specific VeVe fee percentages
> A widely repeated community figure is **2.5% to VeVe plus a licensor fee** (Vevepedia states 2.5% "which goes towards VeVe and its licensors" plus an additional 6% on Disney-licensed items; search snippets attribute a 6.0% Marvel licensor fee to an older version of VeVe's marketplace explainer). VeVe's **current** published fee schedule does not name any secondary-market percentage, and the current "How The VeVe NFT Marketplace Works" post refers only to "the marketplace success fee" shown in the listing interface. Treat 2.5% / 6% as community-sourced and undated, not as a current official rate.

The asymmetry is clean: the open market cannot bind a royalty because anyone can deploy a competing front-end against the same contract, so royalties survive only where the *token itself* enforces them (ERC-721C) or where a single operator controls the venue. VeVe is the second case by construction.

## Liquidity and price discovery

These markets have opposite shapes.

**Open collections are shallow-wide.** One collection, one order book, thousands of near-substitutable units, and bid-side liquidity that barely exists in VeVe: Blur's bid pools, collection-wide offers, NFT lending. The floor is a live two-sided quote, quoted in ETH or SOL, and every front-end sees essentially the same orders. Within a collection, price dispersion is driven by traits — the Solid Gold fur, the Alien punk.

**VeVe is deep-narrow.** ~2,850 collectibles and ~3,856 comic issues each have their own order book, and each is split across two venues in two currencies. Within one collectible, copies are *not* fungible: mint number matters, and low mints carry substantial premiums (see [[Significant Mints]]). So the unit of price discovery is not "a VeVe collectible" but "this collectible at roughly this mint band on this venue."

That fragmentation has a measurable consequence documented in [[platform/floor-prices|Floor Prices]]: many collectibles have **no StackR listing at all**, so they have no StackR floor, and the honest display is `—` rather than an estimate. It also means a single troll-priced ask on an illiquid item becomes "the floor."

Where VeVe is *better* off than it looks: it has real trade prints. This project mirrors **300k+ completed sales since 2025-07-12** across both markets — 302,286 analysed in the current [[platform/record-sales|record-sales]] build. What VeVe lacks is not price history but a public API; the history exists and is attributable per collectible.

## Floor-based market caps are not comparable to trade-based numbers

This is the section to read before putting a VeVe figure next to a PFP figure.

A collection "market cap" as published by NFT trackers is **floor price × total supply**. It is a proxy, and it fails in specific ways:

1. **It assumes every unit is worth the floor.** Never true. In a collection where the rarest units sell for 100× the floor and the median unit sells below it, neither tail is represented.
2. **A floor is a lowest *ask*, not a traded value.** Nobody paid it. On thin books it can be a mispriced or deliberately silly listing — a failure mode this project hit in its own catalogue, where `floor` is a lowest-ask listing that inflates portfolio values on illiquid items.
3. **It ignores the distribution above it.** A 1 ETH floor with listings at 1.01, 1.02, 1.03 is a completely different market from a 1 ETH floor whose next ask is 1.8.
4. **It is sweepable.** Buying out the cheapest listings raises the "market cap" of the whole collection without any change in durable demand.
5. **You could not realise it.** Selling all 10,000 units at the floor is not a transaction that exists.

So the cross-platform snapshots in this wiki's `nft/` pages are labelled explicitly — e.g. CryptoPunks at 2026-07-29: floor **$61,871**, marketcap **$618,342,496** *(floor-based)*. The parenthetical is the whole point. (Note that those two numbers do not multiply out against a 10,000 supply — $61,871 × 10,000 = $618.71M — so even the tracker's own "floor × supply" is computed from a floor captured at a different moment than the one displayed. Another reason not to treat the figure as a value.)

**Volume is not a safe comparator either, because of wash trading.** Documented episodes:

| Case | Figure | Source basis |
|---|---|---|
| LooksRare, Jan 2022 | ~**$4.4B** in fake Meebits volume — the largest single slice of **$8.3B** wash-traded on LooksRare | CryptoSlam, reported 2022-01-28; see [[nft/meebits\|Meebits]] |
| Blur, from 2023-02-14 | **≥$577M** of wash trades in the ~11 days after the token airdrop began | CryptoSlam as of 2023-02-25, via Forkast |
| Blur, share of trades | **~14% vs >80%** depending on methodology — Hildobby's Dune dashboard: $345M, ~14% of volume since Blur's Oct 2022 launch; CryptoSlam, using a wider "inorganic trading" definition: $824M of $1.02B. CryptoSlam put OpenSea at ~2.5% ($6.6M) over the same period | Estimates disagree by ~6× |

The mechanism is incentive: when a marketplace pays a tradeable token for volume, volume becomes the product. VeVe has no tradeable reward token to farm by trading, charges the seller a success fee plus a licensor fee on every sale, and its points economy ([[Master Collector Points|MCP]]) rewards *holding* rather than trading. That makes the wash-trade incentive structurally weaker — **not zero, and not independently audited**, so VeVe volume figures still deserve the same scepticism, just for different reasons (a closed operator-reported book rather than farmable rewards).

### The comparability table

| Metric | Basis | Safe to compare across platforms? |
|---|---|---|
| Floor price | Lowest current **ask** | Only against another floor, same day, same currency convention |
| "Market cap" (floor × supply) | Derived from an ask | **No** — never against a traded-value figure |
| Completed sale price | An actual settled trade | Yes, with the caveat that both sides must be settled trades |
| Record sale | Single highest settled trade | Yes — but state the observation window ([[platform/record-sales\|record sales]] starts 2025-07-12) |
| Lifetime volume | Sum of trades | Only with a wash-trade adjustment stated |
| Drop / list price (Gems) | VeVe **primary** sale price | Not a market value at all; VeVe-specific |
| Holder count | Addresses holding ≥1 | **No** — on Collect Chain the largest holders are platform reserve and store inventory, not collectors; several tracker APIs also cap holder lists |

## What each model is actually good at

**The open model gives you:** self-custody, verifiable fixed supply, a licence you can build a business on (sometimes CC0), one deep order book per collection, bid-side liquidity and lending, and public trade data that anyone can index. It costs you: creator royalties that mostly evaporated, incentive-farmed volume statistics, and art with no pre-existing audience.

**VeVe gives you:** licensed IP people already care about, a per-item primary-sale record (edition size, rarity, Gem list price, reserve, first public mint), an enforced licensor cut that keeps rights-holders in the deal, and a product — 3D/AR viewing, showrooms, a comic reader. It costs you: custody, a non-commercial revocable licence, supply set by the operator, no official public market API, and price discovery fragmented across thousands of tiny two-venue order books.

For the closest structural comparison in the other direction — another licensed walled garden, but one that outsourced its secondary market to open Solana venues — see [[comparisons/veve-vs-candy-digital|VeVe vs Candy Digital]].

concepts/Blind Box.md:
# Blind Box

## Definition

A drop format where you buy a **sealed box** and receive a **randomized** collectible from a defined set — you don't learn the item, rarity, or edition until after purchase. *(high)*

## How It Works

- The set spans multiple [[Rarity and Editions|rarity tiers]] at different odds.
- Generally **better odds** than single-item drops because the combined edition pool is larger.
- A common way VeVe distributes **[[Secret Rare]]** chase items.

## Why It Matters

Blind boxes randomize scarcity, which fuels [[platform/marketplace|marketplace]] trading as collectors buy/sell to complete sets or chase specific pulls.

## Connections
- A kind of → [[Drop Types]]
- Can contain → [[Secret Rare]]

## Sources
- [[catalog-rarity-drops]] (vevepedia.com/terms/blind-box)

concepts/Drop Types.md:
# Drop Types

## Definition

A **drop** is a timed primary release of a new collectible; the **Market** is the secondary resale venue (fixed-price listings + auctions). *(high)*

## Formats

- **Single-item drop** — you select the exact collectible.
- **[[Blind Box]]** — you buy a sealed box and receive a **random** item from the set; rarity/edition unknown until after purchase. Generally better odds than single-item (larger combined pool); used to seed **[[Secret Rare]]s**.
- **Store drops** — items sold directly from the in-app store; post-drop leftovers flow here (~7 min after a drop).

## Waitlist / Queue Mechanics *(high)*

- Waitlist **opens 12 hours before** the drop, **closes 5 minutes before**.
- Reservations are **randomly allocated**; **KYC-verified users get priority** (unverified can still enter).
- Winners get a notification and a **5-minute window** to complete purchase; miss it → reservation forfeited, item returned to public allocation (buyable ~7 min after).
- No need to pre-load [[Gems]] — you can buy Gems at purchase time.

## Why It Matters

Format determines scarcity and strategy: single-item rewards speed + queue luck; blind boxes add chance; the waitlist + KYC priority shape who can acquire limited editions at primary.

## Connections
- Part of → [[platform/drops|drops]]
- Outcomes → [[Rarity and Editions]], [[Secret Rare]]

## Sources
- [[catalog-rarity-drops]] (veve.me/blog/.../veve-waitlist-drops)

concepts/Gems.md:
# Gems

## Definition

**Gems** are VeVe's in-app currency, used to buy [[platform/collectibles|collectibles]] in the Store and on the Market. **1 Gem = US$1.00** in-app value (per VeVe's Terms). *(high)*

## How It Works

- Bought via **credit card, Apple Pay, or Google Pay**; VeVe recommends the web app to avoid app-store fees. *(high)*
- Also obtainable by converting [[OMI Token|OMI]] → Gems on **StackR** ($1 of OMI = 1 Gem, with a 7% OMI burn + 3% fee). *(high)*
- **Non-refundable, non-transferable**, and **(since 19 Nov 2025) non-withdrawable / non-cashable** — a closed-loop currency (VeVe compares it to Roblox/Twitch credits). The former "VeVe Payout" cash-out is gone. *(high)*
- Not a cryptoasset; not on a blockchain. *(high)*

## Why It Matters

Gems are the unit every in-app price is denominated in — collectibles are priced in Gems, never in [[OMI Token|OMI]]. The app's pricing, floor values, and the MCP Optimizer's "cost" side are all in Gems.

## Connections
- Funded by → [[OMI Token]] (via StackR conversion)
- Spent on → [[platform/drops|drops]], [[platform/marketplace|marketplace]]
- Cost basis for → [[Master Collector Points|MCP]] optimization

## Sources
- [[economy-gems-omi-mcp]] (veve.me/terms/terms-for-gems/, veve-fees)

concepts/Master Collector Points.md:
# Master Collector Points

## Definition

**Master Collector Points (MCP)** are VeVe's loyalty/score system under the **Master Collector Program**. Unusually, the **earning formula is published officially** (source: [[economy-gems-omi-mcp]]), which makes it possible to compute exactly — this powers the app's **MCP Optimizer**.

Two parallel tracks:
- **Levels** — permanent, individual, based on *total accumulated* points; 0→100 on an exponential curve. **Exact per-level thresholds are NOT public.**
- **Ranks** — dynamic and **competitive (percentile)**; 22 ranks from **Starter → Master Collector** (Master Collector = **top ~3%**). Ranks can go *down* if peers out-earn you.

MCP points are a **separate currency from [[Gems]]** — you don't buy points, and spending points doesn't lower your Level/Rank.

## How Points Are Earned

### Daily Asset Points (drives Rank — by what you HOLD)
**Collectibles (figures):** base **1.0** each.
- Rarity bonus (added): Rare **+0.25** · Ultra Rare **+0.50** · Secret Rare **+5.00** (Common/Uncommon = base only, no rarity bonus).
- Low-mint bonus: **+0.5** (flat, additive) for the **lowest 5% of editions _available to the public_** — i.e. computed on `(edition − withheld)`, **excluding any editions VeVe retained**. *(Verbatim: "0.5 Points … for the 5% lowest mints available to the public … excludes any Collectibles retained by VeVe.")*
- Duplicate diminishing (same item): 2nd **0.75** · 3rd **0.35** · 4th+ **0.10**.

**Comics (rarity IS the base):** Common **0.25** · Uncommon **0.50** · Rare **2.0** · Ultra Rare **3.0** · Secret Rare **6.0**.
- Low-mint bonus: **+50%** (multiplier on the comic's points) for the lowest 5% of **public** editions (excludes withheld).

> [!note] Verified 2026-06-24 (against `veve.me/blog/veve/mcp/...earning-mcp-points`)
> - **Low mint = lowest 5% of PUBLIC editions, excluding VeVe-retained.** Not the raw total. *(This corrected the engine, which had used total edition size.)*
> - Daily points are applied once/24h; **points stop accruing after 7 days of inactivity** (confirmed).
> - ⚠️ VeVe's page has a self-contradictory parenthetical `(total editions *0.05%)` next to the "5%" prose — the **5% (of public) wording governs**.
- Duplicate diminishing: 2nd **50%** · 3rd **25%** · 4th+ **10%** — **Common & Uncommon comics are EXEMPT** (stack linearly). **No set bonus** for comics.

**Set completion (daily, by set size):** 1→**1.0** · 2→**2.0** · 3→**3.0** · 4→**4.0** · 5+→**5.0**. Duplicate-set diminishing: 2nd **30%** · 3rd **20%** · 4th+ **10%**.

### One-Off Points
Onboarding **+100** · complete a Set **+100** (once per set ever) · Store purchase **+25** · Market purchase **+15**.

### Daily Activity Points
**+1** per in-app action (open/like/comment/share/list/buy), **capped at 25/day**.

### OMI Reward Tier
Holding [[OMI Token|OMI]] in a linked wallet earns **bonus daily points** ∝ OMI held (max 10M eligible). *(exact curve not public)*

## Spending Points (sinks)
Priority Bidding (reserve a drop edition) and Store Accessories; deducted only on a *winning* bid. Real datapoint (VeVe, Jul 2024): a crafting event priced an Ultra Rare at **250,000 MCP** and a Secret Rare at **1,000,000 MCP**.

## Optimization (the cheapest-points logic)
Because the formula is exact, "cheapest points" is arithmetic on floor prices:
- **Secret Rares pay most per item** (6.0/day) but cost most.
- **Collectible duplicates are heavily penalized** (4th+ = 0.10) → breadth > depth.
- **Common/Uncommon comics are duplicate-exempt** → the one linear stacking path.
- **Set completion is efficient** (+100 one-off + up to 5.0/day).
- Rank is holdings-driven; Gem *spend* barely moves it (+25/+15 only).

See the [[architecture|MCP Optimizer spec]] and `app/assets/mcp.js` for the canonical implementation.

> [!warning] Don't overpromise
> Exact Level thresholds and the OMI reward curve are **not public** — the optimizer gives exact *daily points* and *points-per-Gem*, but rank/level projections must stay qualitative. VeVe also reserves the right to change MCP and to act against "gaming the system."

## Connections
- Earned by holding → [[Rarity and Editions|rarities & editions]], completing **Sets**
- Boosted by → [[OMI Token]] holdings
- Currency contrast → [[Gems]]

## Sources
- [[economy-gems-omi-mcp]] (cites veve.me/blog/veve/mcp/*)

# OMI Token

## Definition

**OMI** is the cryptocurrency token of the VeVe / Collect (ex-ECOMI) ecosystem. As of the Nov 2025 changes, OMI is an **external settlement asset, not an in-app currency**. *(high)*

## How It Works

- **Primary utility: convert OMI → [[Gems]] on StackR** at **$1 of OMI = 1 Gem**, with a **7% OMI burn + 3% StackR fee** per conversion (live since 19 Nov 2025). *(high)*
- OMI is **not used inside the VeVe app** — conversion and OMI/NFT trading happen on **StackR** (a separate marketplace on the Base network). *(high)*
- **Indirect in-app benefit:** holding OMI in a linked wallet earns **bonus daily [[Master Collector Points|MCP]]** (OMI Reward Tier, max 10M OMI eligible). *(high)*

> [!warning] Licensor / token flags
> - **"OMI = Collect Chain native/gas token" is UNVERIFIED speculation** — official posts are silent; the only documented OMI-gas relationship is on Base (StackR-sponsored). *(flag)*
> - The old "10% of store revenue buys back & burns OMI" mechanic is **likely superseded** by the 7% conversion burn. *(flag)*

## Why It Matters

OMI is the bridge between the open crypto market and in-app spending. Understanding the OMI→Gem path (and its burn) is key to the "fund my collecting cheaply" question and to the MCP OMI Reward Tier.

## Connections
- Converts to → [[Gems]]
- Boosts → [[Master Collector Points]] (OMI Reward Tier)
- Traded on → StackR (Base)

concepts/Rarity and Editions.md:
# Rarity and Editions

## Definition

Every VeVe collectible is issued as a **limited edition** with a fixed total, and each copy carries a unique **mint number** (e.g. "#100 of 5,000").

## Rarity Tiers (official)

In order from most to least common: **Common · Uncommon · Rare · Ultra Rare · Secret Rare (SR)**. *(high)*
- Not every drop spans all five — some have only 1–2 tiers.
- Rarity is **not** a strict function of edition size; SR editions vary widely (sometimes <100, sometimes >1,000).

## Mint Numbers & "Low Mint"

- Lower mint numbers are scarcer and command premiums. *(medium — community-sourced)*
- VeVe holds back allocation for licensors/marketing, so the **lowest publicly available mint is often #41**. *(medium)*
- Community-observed sub-100 premiums over floor: Common ~10×, Uncommon ~8×, Rare ~6×, Ultra Rare ~4×, SR ~3×; sub-50 ≈ 20–30×. *(directional)*

## Why It Matters

Scarcity drives secondary value, and rarity + low-mint directly drive **[[Master Collector Points|MCP]]**:
- Collectibles: Rare +0.25, Ultra Rare +0.50, **Secret Rare +5.00**/day; **low-mint (lowest 5%) +0.5**.
- Comics: rarity sets the base (Common 0.25 → SR 6.0); low-mint +50%.

## Connections
- Extreme case → [[Secret Rare]]
- Drives → [[Master Collector Points]], floor value ([[platform/economy|economy]])
- Set at → [[platform/drops|drops]]

## Sources
- [[catalog-rarity-drops]] (vevepedia.com/terms/rarity, /low-mint)

concepts/Secret Rare.md:
# Secret Rare

## Definition

**Secret Rare (SR)** is VeVe's top rarity tier — the rarest, fewest-edition variant, often seeded into a [[Blind Box]] as a low-odds chase item. *(high)*

## How It Works

- Smallest editions in a drop (SR sizes vary — sometimes <100, sometimes >1,000).
- Typically commands the highest [[platform/marketplace|marketplace]] prices in its drop.
- **Pays the most [[Master Collector Points|MCP]] per item:** a Secret Rare **collectible** earns **+5.00/day** on top of base (6.0 total); an SR **comic** earns **6.0/day**. *(high)*

## Why It Matters

SRs are the "chase" — the lottery upside that drives blind-box demand and is the single highest daily-MCP item type, which makes cheap-floor SRs a focus of the MCP optimizer.

## Connections
- Top of → [[Rarity and Editions]]
- Hidden inside → [[Blind Box]], [[Drop Types]]
- Max daily points → [[Master Collector Points]]

## Sources
- [[catalog-rarity-drops]], [[economy-gems-omi-mcp]]

concepts/Significant Mints.md:
# Significant Mints

## Definition

A **significant mint** is a specific edition number that collectors prize for reasons beyond its rarity tier — being the first, the lowest public, a milestone, a pattern, or a number with **historical meaning** to the character. The app's **Mint Checker** detects these and can scan a whole collection. Categories are **selectable** so a collector filters by what they care about.

## Selectable categories

| Category | Catches |
|----------|---------|
| **Historically significant** | #1 (the first edition); the lowest public mint; and **character-specific year matches with a reason** (see below) |
| **Lowest mints** | #1, single-digits, the lowest public mint (#41 by VeVe's #1–40 reserve), sub-50, sub-100, MCP low-mint (lowest 5%) |
| **Highest mints** | the final/ceiling mint (#=edition size), near-ceiling (highest 5%) |
| **Palindromes** | #1331, #12321 … |
| **Ascending / descending** | any consecutive run of 3+ digits — #234, #1234, #7654, #9876 (works for any edition size, not gated to start at 1/9) |
| **Patterns & milestones** | repeating digits (#1111), milestones (#5000), round numbers, repeating AB patterns |
| **Meme / iconic numbers** | #69, #420, #1337, #42, #666, #9000, #8008, #80085 |

## Historically significant years (with reasoning)

This is character-specific. A mint number that equals a meaningful year in the character's history is flagged **with the reason**. Examples:
- A **Walt Disney** piece: **#1901** (Walt born) · **#1923** (Disney founded) · **#1955** (Disneyland opened) · **#1966** (Walt died) · **#1971** (Disney World opened).
- **Batman**: **#1939** (first appearance) · **#1940** (Batman #1) · **#1989** (Tim Burton film) · **#1915** (Bob Kane born).
- Licensed film characters can also match the **actor's birth year** (e.g. Luke Skywalker **#1951** — Mark Hamill born) or the **creator's** (e.g. any Marvel character **#1922** — Stan Lee born).

The collectible's own **first-appearance year** is always included (reason: "first appearance"). The per-character year lists are curated and expand over time. Data lives in `app/assets/significant-years.js`; the engine in `app/assets/mints.js`.

## Why it matters

Significant mints command premiums on the secondary [[platform/marketplace|market]] and are a core part of the collector hunt — letting people search their (or any) collection for standout editions is a flagship feature of the community app. The **lowest-public** and **lowest-5%** flags also tie directly into [[Master Collector Points|MCP]] (low-mint bonus).

## Connections
- Builds on → [[Rarity and Editions]]
- Feeds → [[Master Collector Points]] (low-mint bonus)

## Sources
- App engine `app/assets/mints.js` + `significant-years.js` · collector convention (not an official VeVe designation)

domains/dc.md:
# DC

> [!warning] Fact-check pending
> This page was expanded by a research pass on **2026-07-30** with cited sources, but its
> adversarial verification pass **did not run** (the API spend limit was reached mid-workflow).
> The equivalent pass on the `platform/` pages caught a fabricated statistic, a wrong founder
> attribution and a mis-stated first drop — so treat dates, ownership and figures here as
> **provisional** until verified. See [[log]].


## Overview

DC is the publisher that invented the super hero: *Action Comics* #1 (June 1938) introduced Superman, and everything from Batman and Wonder Woman to the Justice League followed from it. Founded as National Allied Publications in the mid-1930s, it has sat under the Warner corporate umbrella since 1967 and inside Warner Bros. Discovery since 2022 — a parent now itself subject to a pending Paramount Skydance takeover (see [Licensing](#licensing)).

DC matters to VeVe more than its catalog size suggests: **Batman: Black & White Series 1 was the very first collectible drop on the platform**, on 14 October 2020, and its Common — *#100 Todd McFarlane Batman* — still holds the highest recorded DC sale. Beyond Black & White, DC on VeVe means **DC Cover Girls**, **DC Artists Alley**, **DC Bombshells**, **Harley Quinn: Red White & Black**, and **DC Battle Statues**.

**On VeVe:** 82 collectibles across 35 sets — browse the [[_index|Collectibles Catalog]] (universe `dc`) or `collectibles.base`.

## History

**Golden Age — the genre gets invented**

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| 1934–35 | Pulp writer **Malcolm Wheeler-Nicholson** sets up **National Allied Publications**. Sources split on the founding year: Britannica says 1934, Wikipedia 1935. |
| **Feb 1935** | ***New Fun* #1** (cover date) — the company's first title, and one of the first American comic books made of all-new material rather than newspaper-strip reprints. |
| **Mar 1937** | ***Detective Comics* #1** — the anthology whose initials became the company's name. |
| 1937 | Short of cash, Wheeler-Nicholson partners with distributor **Harry Donenfeld** and accountant **Jack Liebowitz** to form **Detective Comics, Inc.**; he is bought out soon after. |
| **Jun 1938** | ***Action Comics* #1** — **Superman**, by **Jerry Siegel** and **Joe Shuster**. The first costumed super hero and the template for the entire genre. |
| **May 1939** | ***Detective Comics* #27** — **Batman**, by **Bob Kane** and **Bill Finger**. |
| Oct 1941 | ***All Star Comics* #8** — **Wonder Woman**, by **William Moulton Marston** and **H. G. Peter**. On sale October 1941; cover-dated Dec 1941 / Jan 1942. |
| **30 Sep 1946** | All-American Publications merges into Detective Comics, Inc. to form **National Comics Publications**, later **National Periodical Publications** (publicly traded from 1961). |

**Silver Age to the present**

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| **Oct 1956** | ***Showcase* #4** reinvents the Flash as Barry Allen — conventionally the start of the Silver Age. |
| **1967** | **Kinney National Company acquires National Periodical Publications.** Kinney's entertainment arm is renamed **Warner Communications** in 1972; DC has been under the Warner umbrella ever since. |
| **1977** | The company formally adopts the name it had been called colloquially for decades: **DC Comics**. |
| 1985–86 | ***Crisis on Infinite Earths*** (Marv Wolfman / George Pérez) collapses the multiverse and resets continuity — the first of DC's periodic line-wide reboots. |
| 1993 | The **Vertigo** imprint launches, home to *Sandman*, *Swamp Thing* and *Death* — characters that later reach VeVe. |
| **2005** | DC Direct ships the first **Batman: Black and White** resin statue, *Batman by Eduardo Risso*. The line runs 15+ years; statues are numbered in release order (Risso = #01), and DC marks the 100th with a **Todd McFarlane** design. This is the physical line VeVe's launch drop digitises. |
| 2009 | **DC Entertainment** is formed to run DC across film, TV and games. |
| 2011 / 2016 | ***The New 52*** line-wide relaunch; ***DC Rebirth*** course-corrects it. |
| Apr 2015 | DC's publishing operation relocates from New York to **Burbank, California**. |
| **Apr 2022** | WarnerMedia merges with Discovery; DC lands inside **Warner Bros. Discovery**. |
| **25 Oct 2022** | **James Gunn** and **Peter Safran** are named co-chairmen/CEOs of a new **DC Studios** (effective 1 Nov 2022), consolidating DC film, TV and animation. |
| **11 Jul 2025** | Gunn's ***Superman*** opens the rebooted DC film universe, grossing roughly **$619M** worldwide — the top-grossing super hero film of 2025. |

## Licensing

- **Licensor:** DC
- **Parent:** Warner Bros. Discovery
- **How VeVe records it:** the licensing entity is not written consistently across DC items in this wiki's catalog — 66 read `DC (Warner Bros. Discovery)`, 7 read `Warner Bros. Discovery Global Consumer Products` (WBD's consumer-products arm) and 2 read **`DC Direct`** (the collectibles imprint whose physical statues the launch drop reproduces). All three are the same rights chain.

> [!warning] Licensor flag
> **DC's licensor is stable; its ultimate parent is not.** Warner Bros. Discovery agreed on **27 Feb 2026** to be acquired by **Paramount Skydance** for **$110.9B ($31/share, cash)**. Shareholders approved it **23 Apr 2026**; the DOJ cleared it **12 Jun 2026**; **twelve state attorneys general sued to block it on 13 Jul 2026**; and on **24 Jul 2026** the parties extended the outside closing date to **1 Jun 2027**. WBD's earlier plan (announced **9 Jun 2025**) to split itself into "Warner Bros." and "Discovery Global" was shelved when the company put itself up for auction on **21 Oct 2025**, after competing bids from Paramount Skydance, Netflix and Comcast.
>
> **The deal has not closed.** Warner Bros. Discovery remains DC's parent today, which is why `parent` is filled rather than `# TODO`. If it does close, DC's ultimate parent becomes Paramount Skydance — the same corporate roof already flagged for [[domains/star-trek|Star Trek]] and [[domains/tmnt|TMNT]]. Re-verify this field before citing it.

## On VeVe

**Scale.** 82 collectibles across 35 sets carry `universe: dc` in this wiki's catalog. Of those, **75 items across 30 sets are actually DC-licensed**; the other 7 (the *Feesh Friends* boxes, two *Gekido* artist proofs and a *CYBERCEL Avatar: The Last Airbender* SDCC box) are non-DC items misfiled under the slug — the figures below use the DC-licensed 75. Rarity split: 11 Common, 15 Uncommon, 22 Rare, 20 Ultra Rare, 7 Secret Rare. Seasons 1–7. Drops by year: 15 (2020), 28 (2021), 23 (2022), 4 (2023), 5 (2024).

**The first drop on VeVe — 14 Oct 2020.** *Batman Black & White Series 1*: four statues, one per rarity tier, each digitising a numbered DC Direct original.

| Item | Rarity | Editions | Notes |
|---|---|--:|---|
| *#01 Eduardo Risso Batman* | Ultra Rare | 1,750 | The physical line's #01 (2005) |
| *#86 Becky Cloonan Batman* | Rare | 3,250 | |
| *#97 Joe Madureira Batman* | Uncommon | 5,500 | |
| *#100 Todd McFarlane Batman* | Common | 7,500 | 79.99 Gems; 0 reserved, first public mint **#16**; after McFarlane's *Batman* #423 cover, sculpted by Jonathan Matthews |

> [!note] The "March 2021" confusion
> Contemporaneous press (Bleeding Cool, ComicBook.com, GamesRadar) dates "DC's first Batman NFTs" to **11 March 2021**. That publicity wave actually covers **Series 4** — *#42 Darwyn Cooke*, *#55 Gary Frank*, *#57 Jae Lee* and *#79 Jim Lee Nightwing*, which match this wiki's catalog for 2021-03-11 exactly. Series 1 dropped five months earlier, on 2020-10-14. This resolves the open question flagged in [[platform/veve-history|VeVe History]].

**Lines and sets.**

- **Batman: Black & White S1–S7** (2020-10-14 → 2023-04-23) — 26 collectibles, the platform's longest-running DC line. Plus **four Blue & Yellow variants** dropped on consecutive days 13–16 Dec 2022, two of them Secret Rares at 1,050 editions.
- **DC Bombshells** — *Big Barda* (2020-12-09, 1,044), *Starfire* (2021-01-07, 1,052), then S2 with *Death* and *Harley Quinn Deluxe 2* (2021-06-24).
- **Harley Quinn: Red White & Black S1–S3** (2021-02-11, 2021-10-16, 2022-06-05) — 12 collectibles; S1 holds the scarcest DC editions on the platform.
- **DC Cover Girls S1–S2** (2021-05-27, 2022-02-05) and **DC Artists Alley S1** (2021-12-04) — 12 collectibles between them.
- **DC Battle Statues** — *Batman vs. Killer Croc* (2022-01-23) and *Superman vs. The Flash* (2022-05-07), both Rare at 8,888.
- **Premium singles** — *Superman* (2021-06-17, 8,888), *Bat-Signal* (2022-12-04), *Swamp Thing* (2022-12-18), *Darkseid* (2023-06-25, 1,970), *Green Lantern / Hal Jordan* (2023-08-12, 2,450).
- **Seasonal / event** — *Deck The Halls of Justice* (2022-12-20): three Secret Rares at 978, 973 and 940 editions.
- **The Batman Who Laughs + Dark Robin #1–#3 + DC Dark Nights: Metal Emblem** (2024-01-21) — five items, the most recent DC drop in the catalog.

**Scarcest DC items.** *Harley Quinn — #19 Steve Pugh* (Ultra Rare, **500**) and *#06 Terry Dodson* (Rare, **750**), both RWB S1, 2021-02-11 — the smallest DC editions VeVe has minted. Then the three *Deck The Halls of Justice* Secret Rares (940 / 973 / 978) and *Big Barda* (1,044). At the other end, *#89 Greg Capullo Batman* and *Jim Lee Batman V3* are the largest at **16,800** each.

**Record sales.** Per [[platform/record-sales|Record Sales]], DC accounts for **14,785 completed real sales** in the recorded window (since 2025-07-12). The top three are all launch-era Black & White:

| Price | Item | Date |
|--:|---|---|
| **$10,308** | *#100 Todd McFarlane Batman* (Common) | 2025-10-23 |
| **$10,250** | *#100 Todd McFarlane Batman* (Common) | 2026-05-07 |
| **$5,022** | *#01 Eduardo Risso Batman* (Ultra Rare) | 2026-04-16 |

That a **7,500-edition Common** outsells every Ultra Rare and Secret Rare in the universe is the clearest evidence on the platform that first-drop provenance can outweigh scarcity.

> [!warning] Unverified
> No DC drop appears in this wiki's catalog after **2024-01-21** — roughly two and a half years dormant as of this page's date. Whether that reflects a lapsed or renegotiated licence, a pause during the WBD sale process, or simply a gap in the catalog is `# TODO`; no announcement either way was located.
